To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
case–control data can be analysed efficiently using a linear model with the continuous outcome variable.

(i) the method of Moser and Cooms can be used to obtain more efficient estimates of odds ratios for case–control studies with a binary exposure and a continuous outcome variable; (ii) this method provides more efficient estimates of the odds ratios even when the outcome variable is dichotomized; (iii) gains in statistical efficiency are substantial even for small sample sizes; and (iv) gains in statistical efficiencies for case–control designs are much smaller than for prospective designs.
the use of linear‐model‐analysis methods can lead to large gains in statistical efficiency when analysing case–control studies with continuous outcome variables.

developing a new methodology for the analysis of data from case–control studies, with a continuous outcome.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the case–control design is a very good design for estimating odds ratios, and that the linear‐model‐ based approach is a very good way to estimate odds ratios from a continuous outcome variable.
, when the outcome is continuous, case–control studies are less efficient than cohort studies for estimating odds ratios.
the linear‐model approach provides a more efficient and more robust method for analysing case–control data, with a continuous outcome, than logistic regression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

case–control studies are a very efficient way of estimating odds ratios for binary outcomes and linear‐model‐ based analyses of continuous outcome data are very efficient for case–control studies, too.

the use of linear regression for case–control data is more efficient than the use of logistic regression, and this is true for both the estimation of odds ratios and for the estimation of design‐specific standard errors.
the linear model is a more efficient method than logistic regression for analysing a continuous outcome variable when the outcome is dichotomized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of linear regression for case–control analysis of a continuous outcome variable can be much more efficient than the use of logistic regression.

linear model‐based analyses can be much more efficient than logistic regression analyses when analysing case–control data, and that these gains in efficiency are much smaller when linear model‐based methods are being used than when logistic regression is being used.
linear‐model‐analysis of case–control data can be much more efficient than logistic regression analysis of dichotomized data.
